opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the trickier parts of the policy to get right, and I think it's honestly one of the places where we're still learning.

The basic idea is that we don't want to run our evaluations only once a model is already at the dangerous capability level. By then it's too late. So we try to design the evaluations to trigger at a point that's meaningfully *below* the threshold we actually care about, and we commit to re-running them at regular intervals as we scale up, in terms of effective compute and also as we make algorithmic improvements or post-training changes. The buffer is the gap between "the evals say we're fine" and "the model could actually be dangerous," and you want that gap to be bigger than the jump you might make before you test again.

So how do you judge whether it's big enough? A few things go into it.

One is empirical: how much do capabilities actually move between checkpoints? If you look at scaling trends across past models, you can get a rough sense of how much a given increase in compute tends to improve performance on the relevant tasks. You want the buffer to comfortably cover that, with some margin for the fact that capabilities sometimes jump more than you'd expect from a smooth curve.

A second, and I think more important, is elicitation. When we test a model, we're measuring what *we* can get it to do in a limited amount of time. But after deployment, lots of people will spend much more effort on it, with better prompting, scaffolding, fine-tuning, tools that don't exist yet. So there's a real gap between what we measure and what the model can actually do. Part of the buffer is there to account for that underestimation, and that's harder to quantify. We try to put real effort into elicitation, and treat it as something like red-teaming our own evals, but you never fully close that gap.

Third, there's the question of how sharp the threshold is in the first place. For something like "can this model meaningfully uplift someone trying to make a bioweapon," there isn't one crisp line. So we try to be conservative in where we set the warning signs, and lean toward triggering early, because the cost of a false alarm is mostly that we do more safety work sooner, while the cost of missing it is much worse.

And I'd say the honest answer is that you also judge it retrospectively. Every time we go through this process, we learn things: an eval that saturated faster than we expected, or an elicitation technique that bumped performance more than we'd assumed. That feeds back into the next version of the policy. The RSP is meant to be iterative for exactly that reason. I don't think anyone should claim we've nailed the precise number. The goal is to be clearly on the conservative side and to keep tightening our understanding as we go.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and I'd say the honest answer is that it's a judgment call rather than something we can prove is right.

The basic structure is that we have these capability thresholds, and the idea is you want to catch a model before it crosses a threshold where it'd be dangerous, not after. So the evaluations are deliberately set up to trigger well before the actual dangerous capability. We're not testing "can this model autonomously replicate" or "can it actually help someone make a bioweapon" — we're testing for something much easier that we think would show up first. If the model passes the easier thing, that's your warning sign, and you need the next level of safety measures in place before you keep going.

The question of whether the buffer is big enough really comes down to a few things. One is how fast capabilities move between evaluations. If we're testing every certain amount of compute scaled, we need to be confident that the jump in capability over that interval isn't so large that a model could go from "fails the easy eval" to "actually dangerous" in a single step. And that's genuinely uncertain, because capability jumps aren't perfectly smooth or predictable.

The second thing is elicitation. The scary failure mode isn't that the model can't do the task — it's that the model can do it and we failed to get it to show us. So a lot of the buffer is really there to account for the fact that our evaluations might be underestimating what the model is capable of. Someone with more time, better prompting, fine-tuning, or tool scaffolding might get a lot more out of it than we did. We try to put real effort into elicitation, but I don't think anyone should feel fully confident they've maxed it out.

And then the third thing is just: what's the base rate on us being wrong about where the threshold actually is? Even if the eval is calibrated correctly relative to our model of the risk, our model of the risk could be off.

So how do I actually judge it? Partly by looking at the empirical trends — how much do models improve on these evals from one generation to the next, and is that consistent with the gap we've left. Partly by red-teaming the elicitation question specifically. And partly, honestly, by trying to err conservative. If I'm uncertain whether the buffer is big enough, the answer is to make it bigger, or to test more frequently, rather than to assume it's fine.

I'd also say the policy is designed to be revised. If we learn that the buffer was too small — say a model blows past an eval much faster than expected — that's a signal to update the whole framework, not just to note it and move on. I think that iterative aspect is actually one of the more important parts, because I don't think anyone has this figured out well enough to get it right the first time and leave it alone.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: could the model cross a dangerous capability threshold before the next evaluation catches it? The buffer needs to account for both how much capabilities might improve between evaluations and how uncertain the evaluations themselves are.

So I’d want to ask: if progress were faster than we expected, or our tests were underestimating what the model could do, would we still have enough warning to put the required safeguards in place? You also need to consider whether additional training or better ways of eliciting capabilities could reveal something your initial evaluation missed.

I don’t think you can establish that the buffer is sufficient just by specifying a fixed interval between tests. You need evidence that the evaluations give you an early enough signal, and you need to revisit the interval as you learn more. If you can’t make a convincing case that you’ll detect the threshold before crossing it, you should evaluate more frequently or use a more conservative trigger.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: could the model cross a threshold before the next evaluation detects it? So you need to account for how quickly capabilities might improve, how long it takes to run and interpret the evaluations, and how much uncertainty there is in what those evaluations actually measure.

If you evaluate a model and it falls short of a dangerous capability threshold, that’s only reassuring if the evaluations are sensitive enough to detect that capability when it’s present. A model failing to do something with the prompting and tools you tried isn’t necessarily evidence that it couldn’t do it with better scaffolding or more effort.

So I’d want the buffer to accommodate plausible capability improvements and uncertainty in the measurement, with enough time to put the required safeguards in place before crossing the threshold. And I wouldn’t treat that as something you establish once. As you learn more about how capabilities develop and how reliable your evaluations are, you should revisit it. If you can’t justify the buffer, you need more frequent evaluations or a more conservative stopping point.
